text: Sabon is an old-style serif typeface designed by German-born typographer Jan Tschichold (1902–1974) between 1964 and 1967. It was released in 1967 by the Linotype, Monotype, and Stempel type foundries. The roman style is based on types by Claude Garamond (c. 1480–1561), specifically a specimen printed by Frankfurt printer Konrad Berner, who married the widow of Jacques Sabon, the source of the face's name, and had acquired some of Garamond's type after his death. The italics are based on types designed by Robert Granjon, a contemporary of Garamond. Sabon is effectively a Garamond revival, though a different name was chosen because many other modern typefaces already use the name Garamond. Tschichold was commissioned by a coalition of German printers to create a typeface that would print identically on Linotype, Monotype, or letterpress equipment, simplifying line planning and pagination. The italic and bold styles were required to take up exactly the same space as the roman, a feature dictated by the duplexing system of Linotype hot metal typesetting machines, where each matrix casts two characters (e.g., roman or italic, roman or bold) of equal width. The font was also designed to be five per cent narrower than the existing Monotype Garamond to save space and money. The name "Sabon" was proposed by Stanley Morison, an influential British Monotype artistic advisor and historian of printing. Tschichold used an Egenolff-Berner specimen sheet from 1592 as a model, selecting a Garamond face for the roman and a Granjon face for the italics. Different drawings were used for machining larger sizes. Sabon was first used in the 1973 Washburn College Bible, set by Bradbury Thompson using thought-unit typography. It was also used in the 1979 Book of Common Prayer of the Episcopal Church (United States) and all of its secondary liturgical texts. In the 2000s, Sabon served as the official logo typeface of Stanford University until 2012 and is used by Örebro University alongside Trade Gothic. Vogue and Esquire use a slightly modified version for headlines. Since 2010, First Things has used Sabon for page text in its print edition, and the Incorporated Council of Law Reporting uses it for its Law Reports. Digital versions of Sabon are available from Linotype and Monotype; Monotype Sabon is lighter than the Linotype version. Linotype also released Sabon Georgian and Sabon Paneuropean with extended language support. Adobe offered a version called Adobe Sabon, but it is not widely available as of 2022. Fontsite released a version named Savoy, and Bitstream released a less faithful version named Classical Garamond. Jean-François Porchez designed Sabon Next, a revival based on Tschichold's 1967 Sabon design for Stempel and Porchez's study of original Garamond and Le Bé models. Unlike the original, Sabon Next rejects a matching-width italic in favor of a more traditional design, narrower than the roman, and takes advantage of digital typesetting to include a wide 'f' in the sixteenth-century style. The commercial version is commonly called Sabon Next LT Pro or Sabon Next Pro. Sabon Next Pro includes six weights (Display, Regular, Demi, Bold, Extra Bold, and Black), though the 'Display' weight is considered a grade of the 'Roman' weight and recommended for 11pt or above, while the 'Regular' weight is designed for smaller sizes like 8pt. The font includes Latin Extended characters but lacks Greek and Cyrillic support. OpenType features include Small caps (except in Black), Ligatures, Special ligatures, Alternates, Caps figures, Oldstyle figures, Tabular figures, Fractions, Superiors, Ornaments, Swash, Proportional Lining figures, and a collection of printers' ornaments and dingbats, which are also available as a separate font named Sabon Next Ornaments. Users of Microsoft Office can download the Regular and Bold weights via cloud fonts as Sabon Next LT, without the 'Pro' label. This version includes support for Greek, Cyrillic, and Turkish characters, though some OpenType features (e.g., stylistic sets and alternative numeric figures) are not available. Sabon eText is a screen-optimized version designed by Steve Matteson, featuring increased x-heights, heavier hairline and serifs, wider inter-character spacing, more open counters, and adjusted thick-to-thin ratios. The family includes four fonts in two weights (regular, bold) with complementary italics, and OpenType features include case-sensitive forms, fractions, ligatures, lining/old style figures, ordinals, superscript, small capitals.
